sentences.text: The single species of this genus is known only from a partial skull that includes the snout, lower jaw, and part of the braincase.
This holotype skull measures about three centimeters in length, and fused bones show the individual was skeletally mature when it died.
Three or four tooth pairs sit in the premaxilla, while the lower jaw displays three visible pairs restricted to the front of the snout.
Fossils were found at the Las Hoyas site in Cuenca, Spain, and the specimen is now kept at the Museo Paleontológico de Castilla-La Mancha.
The name honors Greek myths, linking the genus to Medusa and the specific name to a bird-like figure with an elongated beak.
Its rostrum is about two and a half times the length of the eye orbit, a trait seen in longipterygids, a group previously known only from China.
Skull anatomy suggests it belongs to Longipterygidae, which contains two subfamilies, yet it shows a unique mix of traits from both.
Scientists treat its placement within the family with caution because many defining features of the group are found in the postcranial skeleton, which is missing here.
This animal lived during the Barremian age of the Early Cretaceous, roughly 129.4 million years ago.
The exact relationships of this bird with other longipterygids remain debated due to its mosaic of traits from both longipterygines and longirostravines.
